Frederick William Beechey, “The Harbour of San Francisco, Nueva California,” Hydrographical Office of the Admiralty, 1833.

Source: [David Rumsey Map Collection](https://www.davidrumsey.com/luna/servlet/detail/RUMSEY~8~1~291131~90062697:The-Harbour-of-San-Francisco%2C-Nueva?sort=Pub_List_No_InitialSort%2CPub_Date%2CPub_List_No%2CSeries_No&qvq=q:beechey;sort:Pub_List_No_InitialSort%2CPub_Date%2CPub_List_No%2CSeries_No;lc:RUMSEY~8~1&mi=4&trs=43)

Frederick William Beechey’s navigational chart is the first map to employ modern cartography in a survey of San Francisco Bay. It is thus the first map of San Francisco that can be said to be accurate, in the sense that it corresponds closely with satellite imagery.

In 1825 the British Royal Navy gave command of the HMS Blossom to [Frederick William Beechey, and tasked him with exploring the Bering Strait](https://archive.org/details/narrativeofvoyag00beec/page/n9/mode/2up). Beechey was to “cooperate with the English arctic expeditions under Sir William Parry and Sir John Franklin” (Harlow, 372). A secondary purpose of his voyage was “to improve the surveys of both [James] Cook and [George] Vancouver,” who had produced the first English charts of the West Coast of North America (Harlow, 372). As the arctic winter settled in, the Blossom headed south, arriving in San Francisco Bay on November 6, 1826.

The Mexican War of Independence had concluded in 1821, and the new regime had a policy of accommodating foreign expeditions. Mexican officials gave “every assistance” to Beechey and his crew, asking only that a copy of the chart be left with them upon the conclusion of their work (Beechey, Chapter XIII; Harlow, 372). [Beechey’s account of his stay](https://archive.org/details/narrativeofvoyag00beec/page/344/mode/2up) contains many observations that are of use to historians, particularly his portrayal of the remnants of the Mission system, which he described with unsparing candor. The “remaining inmates of the mission” in San Francisco, he wrote, “were in as miserable a condition as it was possible to conceive” (Beechey, 358).

After a nearly two-month stay, Beechey departed on December 28, 1826. The British Hydrographical Office of the Admiralty published Beechey’s map in 1833. (Derek Hayes’s *Historical Atlas of California* reproduces manuscript versions of the map from 1827.) The historian Neal Harlow writes that the chart marked the dawn of the “modern period in the cartography of the San Francisco Bay” (372). The process of georeferencing historic maps bears out this observation. Attempts at georeferencing Vancouver’s survey, for example, produce images that are so distorted as to be unintelligible. Beechey’s survey, by contrast, corresponds remarkably well to modern satellite imagery. Subsequent surveys of the San Francisco Bay–like Eugene Duflot de Mofras’s 1844 map–relied heavily on Beechey’s work. Beechey’s chart remained the most accurate until the US Coast Survey’s first map of 1853.

The only clear error on Beechey’s map is the Carquinez Strait, which is here shown to be fed by three rivers, labeled “Rio Jesus Maria,” “Rio Sacramiento,” and “Rio San Joachin.” According to Harlow, this was the only physical area that Beechey’s party did not survey in person, relying instead on descriptions given to them by local officials. Duflot’s map is clearly derivative of Beechey’s [except in this detail](https://www.imaginedsanfrancisco.org/maps-and-plans#), where he showed the Strait connecting to the “Baie de los Carquines” (today Suisun Bay) which was in turn fed by only two rivers, the “Río del Sacramento” and the “Río San Joaquín.”

Beechey’s map employed a number of place names that have since changed. “Paps,” for example, is an archaic geographic term referring to breast-shaped hills, here Twin Peaks. (The Spanish also referred to Twin Peaks as “*[pechos](https://www.loc.gov/resource/g4364s.pm000332/)*,” or breasts.) Mt. Tam is here shown as “Table Hill.” “Blue Mountain” describes the modern-day Mt. Davidson. “Silver Hummock” appears to describe Pacific Heights.

Another notable feature of Beechey’s map is the road system connecting the Presidio, the pueblo of Yerba Buena, and the Mission. The road between the last two settlements would eventually move to the south, becoming the Mission Plank Road, which defined the eventual course of Market Street, and the otherwise incongruous orientation of the South of Market grid.
